name: Lukey
tagline: He's been dripping for you since 1987.

romance_success.title: Head Over Heels Over Pipes
romance_success.text: Lukey finished the job and didn't clock out. He's still a little damp, still terrible with a wrench, and still singing Bon Jovi off-key at the stove. The kitchen passed inspection. Your heart did not.

romance_failure.title: Love You to the Bottom of the Pool
romance_failure.text: He loved you. That's how he knew it was time to go. Lukey passed on with a kiss on your forehead and one perfect drop of water that never hit the floor. Some nights the faucet hums a little Bon Jovi, just for you.

friend_success.title: Pipe Dreams Come True
friend_success.text: Coach Lukey Moretti finished the job, gave his kid the best birthday present 39 years late, and passed on with a goofy salute and one last splash. The dishwasher has been forgiven. Mostly.

friend_failure.title: Fixed It Myself (Mostly)
friend_failure.text: Lukey passed on a little grumpy, a lot proud, and fully convinced he did all the work. ('You held the flashlight.') The kitchen is dry. Dan got his goggles. A job is a job.

lines: *A gush of water. A gurgle. A very large, very damp man rises out of the cabinet under the sink like a disappointed genie.*
Whoa, whoa, WHOA. Put the wrench down, lady.
I'm the [pipe] around here. Thirty-nine years of drip-drip-drippin', and nobody touches the merchandise.

choices.text: You're a... pipe. That talks.
Funny. You don't look like a pipe. You look like a snack.
I don't care what you are. You're getting fixed.

lines: Copper. Half-inch. Classic 1987 install.
Okay, the install was a little rushed. Gary was a cowboy. Point is, I'm vintage, lady. I'm a collector's item.

choices.text: You're a... pipe. That talks.
Collector's item, huh? You look more like a snack.
Vintage means old. Old means replaced.

lines: Talks, sings, judges your dishwashing technique. I'm a full-service pipe.
You: Does the full-service pipe have a name?
Lukey. Just Lukey. Don't know where I got it. Pipes don't usually get names. I figure I'm special.
*The dripping speeds up. Drip-drip-drip-drip-drip.*
...It's humid in here. Shut up.
Name's Lukey. Not that it matters, lady. You won't be around long enough to need it.
*He sprays you. Directly in the face. With incredible precision.*
Oops. Pressure problem. Should get somebody to look at that.
Name's Lukey. Remember it, 'cause I'm gonna be the reason you sell this dump at a loss.
So what's your deal? You some kinda plumber?

choices.text: I'm a house flipper. I buy broken houses and make them beautiful.
I'm the woman who owns this house now. Including you.
I'm the one with thirty days before the city bulldozes this place.

lines: A flipper! Like a dolphin?
You: Like real estate.
Oh. So a land shark. Great. Love that for the house.
*He crosses his arms. Water pours off his elbows.*
Including me, huh? Bold. I like bold. I don't like YOU, but I like bold.
Bulldozes?! The whole house?
*For one second, the drip stops completely.*
...Okay. That's— whatever. Pipes don't get scared. That's a known fact.
Let me guess. Step one of the big flip: fix the leak.
You: The inspector says it's priority number one.
Yeah, well, here's a news flash, lady. You fix the leak, you fix ME. And a fixed pipe is a dead pipe.
Er. A quiet pipe. Either way, I'm out. So, no thanks.

choices.text: I'm sorry. I didn't know fixing it would hurt you.
Honestly? A quiet Lukey sounds great.
Or maybe you'd be even better without the drip.

lines: *He blinks. A single drop rolls off the end of his nose.*
...Huh. Nobody's ever apologized to the plumbing before.
Don't get mushy on me. I'm still flooding your shoes.
*Lukey will remember that.*
QUIET? I'll show you quiet.
*Every faucet in the house turns on at once.*
That was me. All me. Tremble, lady.
Better? What's better than a drip? A drip is perfect. A drip is RHYTHM.
*He drums on the counter. Water goes everywhere.*
You: You'd be dry. You could sit on a couch.
A COUCH? Lady, I don't even know if I have a—
*He looks down. He definitely has legs. He seems surprised about it.*
*Lukey will remember that.*
Hey, who was that guy with the clipboard on Friday? Windbreaker. Real corny.
Looked right at me and said 'This kitchen's got a real [drip personality|drip].' Pfft. That's MY material.
Who does this guy think he is, stealing my bits?

choices.text: That's Inspector Dan. He decides whether this house lives.
Honestly? His joke was better than yours.
Wait. Are you jealous of the inspector?

lines: 'Drip personality.' That's a classic. I invented that.
I think. I don't remember inventing it. But it FEELS like mine. Like a sock you know is yours.
Dan. Huh. Dan the Man with the Plan and the Clipboard.
Well, you tell Dan the Man the pipe says hi. Actually, don't. Pipes don't say hi.
*A gasp. A real, wet gasp.*
BETTER than mine?! I'll have you know I've been workshopping that bit for thirty-nine years.
...Okay, his delivery was good. I hate it.
Jealous? Of a guy in a windbreaker? Please.
*Drip. Drip. Dripdripdrip.*
...Is he single? Not that I care. Asking for the house.
*He glares across the kitchen at the brand-new dishwasher you installed this morning.*
And who's HE?

choices.text: That's the new dishwasher. Be nice.
Your replacement.
Nobody compared to you, obviously.

lines: Nice? To HIM? With his little buttons and his 'eco mode'? He gets nice when he earns nice.
*The dishwasher door falls open on its own. Lukey looks extremely innocent.*
Whoops. Gravity. Weird stuff, gravity.
*The drip slows to something almost... shy.*
Yeah, well. Obviously. He doesn't even have a face.
*You hold out your hand to shake on it. Your fingers pass right through his, cold and tingly, like reaching into a sink.*
Huh. Weird. That never happened with Gary.
Okay, lady, go do your flippy business. I'll be here. Leaking. Spitefully.
*He sinks back toward the cabinet, then stops.*
Hey... what's a '[Danny]'? I just said it. In my head. I don't know why I said it.
*He frowns at the faucet like it owes him money.*
Probably a brand of pipe fitting. Danny Fittings. Very reliable. Forget I said anything.
Hey, boss. Before you say anything.
Nobody ever apologized to me before last week. I thought about it the whole time. Don't let it go to your head.
Hey, boss. I've been thinking about that couch thing you said.
Sitting. On a couch. Like a guy. I don't even know what my butt looks like. Anyway. Forget it. Don't forget it.
Oh. It's you. I flooded your shoes twice this week. You're welcome.
...Fine. Truce. For tonight. Only 'cause I'm bored.
*The power's out across the whole block. The only light in the kitchen is the soft blue glow of the leak.*
Evening, boss. Blackout. Not me. For once.
Also, those podcast ladies said there's a MERMAID in the plumbing. I'm flattered. I'm not a mermaid. But I'm flattered.
Anyway. You hungry? I got an idea. Candles. Dinner. Me directing. You doing all the actual cooking.

choices.text: Wait. Is this a date?
Sure. Teach me something, Chef Pipe.
You can't even hold a spoon.

lines: *The leak goes drip-drip-drip-drip-drip.*
A DATE? With who? Me? I'm a pipe. Pipes don't— it's a WORKING dinner. Strictly professional, plumbing-adjacent cuisine.
Finally, she wants to learn. Step one: you need a pot. Step two: I fill the pot.
*He fills the pot. And the counter. And your sock.*
Look at that. Teamwork.
Can't hold a spoon. Wow. Okay. You know what I CAN hold?
*A perfectly aimed stream of water knocks your spoon into the sink.*
A grudge.
*You light candles. He talks you through boiling pasta. He is extremely, confidently wrong about how long that takes.*
Okay, now the secret ingredient. You gotta— wait.
*He sniffs the air.*
Do you smell [cake]?

choices.text: There's no cake, Lukey. Are you okay?
Maybe pipes have birthdays too.
Focus. The pasta's burning.

lines: Chocolate. With the rainbow sprinkles. The cheap kind that taste like crayons.
Why do I KNOW that? Pipes don't eat cake. Pipes don't eat anything. Pipes barely even have hobbies.
I'm fine. I'm a pipe. Pipes are always fine.
*The drip goes quiet. Completely quiet. That's new.*
...I think I'm remembering something, boss. And it's freaking me out a little.
Pipes having birthdays. Ha. That's crazy talk.
*Beat.*
If I DID have a birthday, I'd want the crayon sprinkles. Just saying. For the record.
Right. Right. The pasta. The very real, very non-birthday pasta.
*He's clearly still thinking about the cake.*
*While you drain the pasta, something rattles loose behind the cabinet: a battered yellow Walkman, a tape still inside.*
You: Is this yours?
Pipes don't have Walkmans. ...Press play anyway.
*It's Bon Jovi. Lukey knows every single word. He sings all of them. Badly. With choreography.*

choices.text: Sing along with him.
Lukey... you were a person once, weren't you?
That was objectively terrible singing.

lines: *You belt the chorus together. He's off-key. You're off-key. The candles flicker. It's the best bad duet in history.*
...Boss. You're not supposed to be FUN. Nobody told me the landlord would be fun.
*Lukey will remember that.*
*He freezes mid air-guitar.*
A person. Like with a social security number? A haircut?
*He touches the back of his neck like he's checking for something. There is, very faintly, a mullet.*
...I'm gonna need a minute, boss.
TERRIBLE? That was a TRIBUTE. Jon himself would weep.
You: He would. For different reasons.
*He laughs so hard the faucet hiccups.*
*Dinner's done. The candles are low. Without thinking, you reach for his hand on the counter.*
*It doesn't pass through this time. It feels like cold water running between your fingers.*
...Whoa. Did you feel that?

choices.text: I did. Don't let go.
You're getting more solid. That's good, right?
Pull your hand back. 'Sorry. That was weird.'

lines: *He doesn't let go. The drip slows to almost nothing.*
*He looks scared. He also looks really, really happy.*
Good? I dunno, boss. Pipes aren't supposed to get MORE of anything. Except rust.
*But he flexes his wet fingers like he's seeing them for the very first time.*
Yeah. Weird. Totally weird. Super weird.
*Drip.*
...It wasn't THAT weird.
*Your phone buzzes. Your realtor. You step into the hall, but the pipes run through every wall in this house.*
You: Yeah, the kitchen's the last big fix. Once the leak's gone, we list it by the end of the month. Easy money.
*When you come back, the candles are out. Lukey is a cold, hard puddle of attitude.*
'Easy money.' That's what I am? Your easy money?

choices.text: It's my job, Lukey. But you're not just a job to me.
You knew I was flipping this house.
You're right. I should have told you myself.

lines: Not just a job? You were gonna fix me and SELL me. Like a used car. With a mullet.
*He's spraying. Not on purpose. He can't stop.*
I need some time, boss. Please go.
Yeah. I did. Guess I forgot for a second. Guess the candles made me stupid.
*Every faucet in the house shuts off at once. The silence is worse than the drip.*
...Yeah. You should've.
*The spray softens back into a drip.*
I'm still mad, boss. Gimme a few days to be a mad pipe.
*He sinks back under the sink. Just before he's gone, you hear him mutter.*
If you fix me... where does a pipe go?
*The leak is barely a drip today. Lukey is sitting on top of the dishwasher, of all places, staring at the floor.*
You came back. Even after I went full burst-main on you.

choices.text: Of course I came back. I'm not just here for the house.
We're a team. Teams have bad days.
I came back because the leak's still on the inspection list.

lines: *The drip stops. Completely. He looks up at you, and his whole face goes soft and dumb.*
...Okay. Okay, sweetheart. I'm sorry I sprayed you. Emotionally AND literally.
*He just called you sweetheart. He heard it too. He decides not to take it back.*
A team. Yeah. Me and you. The Pipe and the Flipper. Sounds like a buddy cop show.
I'm sorry I lost my cool, sweetheart. A pipe's supposed to stay cool. It's in the job description.
...Right. The list. Course.
*He nods too many times.*
Let's get you your gold star, boss.
Did you hear Bev and Trish? They said a man in [short shorts|shorts] died in this house. In 1987.
*He looks down at his jeans. For a second they're short shorts. Then they're jeans again.*
I think it was me. I think I used to be a guy.

choices.text: I think so too. Do you remember anything else?
For what it's worth, the shorts worked.
Bev and Trish also think you're a mermaid.

lines: Short shorts were IN, Trish. They were IN.
*He spins to show you. Water flies everywhere.*
Bits and pieces. A whistle. Chlorine. A bunch of kids yelling 'Coach! Coach!'
I think I was a swim coach. Me. A guy who is now ninety percent water. That's either poetic or a really bad joke.
1987, baby. Nobody had legs like these. I'm assuming. I'm a little see-through, so it's hard to check.
...Seriously, though. I had a whistle. Chlorine. Kids yelling 'Coach!' I think I was somebody.
Which, still flattered.
But no. I had a whistle. A clipboard. A bunch of kids yelling 'Coach!' I think I was a swim coach.
*Friday. Inspector Dan comes by with his clipboard. Under the sink, the drip goes very, very still.*
*Dan crouches, looks at the pipe and grins. 'Well, would you look at that. This kitchen's got a real drip personality.'*
*After he leaves, Lukey rises out of the cabinet slowly. He looks like he's seen a ghost, which is rich, coming from him.*
...That's MY joke. Why does he have MY joke?

choices.text: Lukey... how old would your kid be now?
Maybe great minds think alike?
It's a pretty common joke, Lukey.

lines: My kid. I had a— I HAD A KID.
*Every faucet in the house turns on at once. Not angry. Overwhelmed.*
Danny. Danny Moretti. Gap in his teeth. Scared of the deep end.
Dan. DAN. That's my Danny. My kid has a CLIPBOARD.
Great minds, sure. Except I taught that joke to somebody. Somebody short. With a gap in his teeth.
*His eyes go wide.*
Danny. My son's name was Danny. And Dan— Dan is— oh my god. My kid has a CLIPBOARD.
Common? That joke is NOT common. That joke is hand-crafted.
I made it up for— for my son. For Danny.
*He sits down hard on the floor. Water pools around him.*
Dan's my kid. My kid grew up without me.
*The radio on the counter crackles. 'BIG STORM SATURDAY. Residents in low-lying areas should prepare for flooding.'*
*Lukey flinches like the word hurt.*
Flooding. Water. Under the sink. There was a party. There was a cake.

choices.text: Sit down next to him. 'Tell me about the party.'
You don't have to remember it all right now.
We don't have time for this. The storm's coming.

lines: No, I wanna. It's like knowing a song but not the words. I gotta get the words.
*He nods fast.*
Right. Right. Storm prep. Sandbags. Pipe stuff.
*But the memory comes anyway, whether you have time for it or not.*
Danny's eighth birthday. Chocolate cake, crayon sprinkles. A clown named Mr. Giggles who smelled like cigarettes.
The sink sprang a leak right before the candles. I said 'Two seconds, buddy!' and dove under there with a wrench.
And I slipped. On the puddle. And I bonked my head on the U-bend.
*A long pause.*
Of all the ways to go. Under a SINK. In front of a CLOWN.
I missed the candles. Danny blew out his candles, and I was under a sink.
*The leak isn't dripping now. It's crying. Quietly.*

choices.text: Take his hand.
Danny turned out great. He became an inspector so no house would ever hurt anyone again.
At least it's kind of a funny way to go?

lines: *You reach for his hand. This time it doesn't feel like water. It feels like a hand. Warm. Calloused. Real.*
*He stares at your fingers in his like they're the eighth wonder of the world.*
...That's the first thing I've held in thirty-nine years that wasn't a wrench.
He did that? Because of— because of ME?
*He laughs and sobs at the same time. It comes out as a gargle.*
My kid's a hero with a clipboard. Course he is. He got the brains from his mom.
*Beat.*
*Then he laughs. A real, big, booming laugh.*
It IS, isn't it? Mr. Giggles probably dined out on that story for years. 'The time the dad died under the sink.' Great bit.
...Still kinda hurts, though.
I think I'm stuck here 'cause I never finished something.
I don't know what it is yet. But I think I need you to help me finish it.
And I think we're gonna need a better wrench.
*Saturday. The sky outside is the color of a bruise. Lukey is waiting by the sink, sleeves rolled up.*
{player}.
*It's the first time he's ever said your real name. He looks like he's been practicing.*
...Too much? I've been workshopping it. You look like a {player}.
*Saturday. The sky outside is the color of a bruise. Lukey is waiting by the sink, sleeves rolled up.*
Hey, boss. Big day.
Did you hear Bev and Trish this week? They interviewed the [clown]. MR. GIGGLES. He remembered me!
Said I owed him twenty bucks. I did NOT owe him twenty bucks. ...I owed him ten.

choices.text: You absolutely owed him twenty bucks.
I'm proud of you. You're remembering everything.
Focus, Lukey. There's a storm coming.

lines: Fifteen. Final offer. He made a balloon dog that looked like a sad potato.
*He's grinning. A whole week ago he didn't remember he had teeth.*
*The drip goes drip-drip-drip-drip. He doesn't even pretend it's the humidity this time.*
Yeah? ...Yeah. Me too. It's nice, having a whole person's worth of stuff in my head again. Even the clown.
Right. Storm. Focus. I'm focused. I'm a laser. A wet laser.
*He is not focused. He is still mad about the twenty bucks.*
He said, and I quote, 'Nicest dad I ever worked a party for. Terrible with a wrench.'
That's going on my tombstone. Do I have a tombstone? Somebody check.
Okay. Before the storm hits. I remembered what I never finished.
Behind the cabinet. Top left. Taped up. Grab it.
*You reach behind the cabinet and find a soggy little package in birthday paper. Inside: kid-sized swim goggles and a card in truly awful handwriting.*
*'HAPPY 8TH DANNY!! This summer I'm teaching you the deep end. Love you to the bottom of the pool and back. — DAD'*

choices.text: Lukey... he never got this.
Your handwriting is genuinely a crime.
Hug him.

lines: Nope. Thirty-nine years behind a cabinet. Worst delivery service in history.
We're gonna fix that. Right after we fix THIS.
My handwriting is ARTISANAL.
*He's laughing. His eyes are wet. Everything about him is wet, but this is different.*
We're giving it to him. Today. But first—
*You hug him. He's solid enough to hug back now. He smells like chlorine and old cassette tapes.*
...Okay. Okay. Don't make me cry. I'm already a leak.
*The storm hits. Rain hammers the windows. The old pipe shudders, groans and starts to spray.*
Okay, listen up, rookie! Righty-tighty! Lefty-loosey is how I DIED!
*You get under the sink together. He can't hold the wrench, but he can see every bolt and every crack from the inside. You're his hands. He's your eyes.*

choices.text: Talk me through it, Coach.
I trust you. Tell me where.
I've got this. I don't need your help.

lines: COACH. She called me Coach. Okay! Quarter turn! Now the compression nut! Breathe! Kick from the hips!
That last one's for swimming. Ignore that one.
*He puts his hands over yours on the wrench. Bolt by bolt. His voice stays steady and soft the whole time.*
There. Feel that? That's the last one. You did it.
*You do it yourself. It takes three tries and a lot of swearing. He hovers, hands half-raised, not quite helping.*
...You held the wrench right. I'll give you that.
*Thunk. Squeak. Silence.*
*Outside, the storm rages. Inside, for the first time in thirty-nine years, the kitchen is completely, beautifully dry.*
*Lukey looks down at himself. He isn't dripping. He's glowing, softly, like a nightlight.*
*Monday. The storm has passed. Inspector Dan arrives for the final inspection and finds the kitchen bone dry.*
*Before he signs off, you hand him the soggy little package. He opens it. He reads the card.*
*He laughs. Then he cries. Then he laughs again, with a gap in his grown-up teeth.*
*Behind him, by the sink, Lukey watches. Finally, finally finished.*
*After Dan leaves, Lukey turns to you. He's shimmering at the edges, like he could go any time he wants.*
So. Job's done. I think I get to pick now. Stay or go.
What do you think I should do?

choices.text: Stay. With me. I love you, Lukey.
I love you. And that's why I think you should go.
Go. You've earned it, Coach. I'll miss you.
That's your call, Lukey.

lines: *He kisses you. A real one. Warm, solid, a little damp and entirely worth thirty-nine years.*
I finished the job, {player}. Doesn't mean I gotta clock out.

v4_rs2.fxText: The storm was over. The kitchen was dry. Nothing else was.
lines: *Later. Much later.*
Best. Repair. Ever.
*He kisses your forehead. Soft. Final.*
I love you too. That's how I know I gotta go. You deserve a guy with a pulse.
And I wanna see what's past the deep end.
*He fades, smiling, into a single perfect drop of water that never hits the floor.*
*He gives you a goofy two-finger salute. It splashes, just once, for old times' sake.*
Thanks, rookie. Best assistant coach I ever had. Tell the dishwasher he's okay. Don't tell him I said that.
*He's gone. Outside, Dan pauses at his car, touches a drop of water on top of his head and grins.*
*He looks at you for a long, long time.*
*Then he decides.*
Hey, gorgeous. Need anything tightened? Loosened? I'm flexible.
*He winks. It is, for once, completely dry.*
*The sink is quiet. Bone dry. Somewhere, very faintly, a faucet hums a little Bon Jovi.*
*The sink is quiet. On the counter, the yellow Walkman is still here. You press play. Bon Jovi. Of course.*
*The sink is dry. Taped to the cabinet, in awful handwriting: 'FIXED IT MYSELF. MOSTLY. YOU HELD THE FLASHLIGHT. — L'*
